masm8086.title: MASM 8086 Mode: Bit Manipulation, Registers and Segments
masm8086.intro: This mode assembles and single-steps real-mode 8086 assembly, so every bit operation is visible as a change in a register, a flag or a memory byte.
masm8086.purpose: The editor executes MASM source one instruction at a time and shows the result in the Registers and Flags, Execution Trace, Stack and Main Memory tabs. Bit manipulation on the 8086 is done with the logic instructions $\texttt{OR}$, $\texttt{AND}$, $\texttt{XOR}$, $\texttt{TEST}$, $\texttt{SHL}$ and $\texttt{SHR}$, which are the direct hardware counterparts of the C idioms for set, clear, toggle and read: $\texttt{REG |= (1UL << n)}$ is an $\texttt{OR}$, $\texttt{REG \&= \textasciitilde(1UL << n)}$ is an $\texttt{AND}$ with the complement mask, $\texttt{REG \textasciicircum= (1UL << n)}$ is an $\texttt{XOR}$, and $\texttt{(REG >> n) \& 1UL}$ is a $\texttt{SHR}$ or a $\texttt{TEST}$.

model.heading: Mask algebra on a register
model.body: A single bit position $n$ is selected by the mask $2^{n}$. Setting uses a bitwise OR, clearing uses an AND with the complement $\sim 2^{n}$, and toggling uses an XOR, so each operation touches exactly one bit and leaves the other bits of the operand unchanged. For an eight-bit register the valid range is $0 \le n \le 7$, and for a sixteen-bit register it is $0 \le n \le 15$.

model.heading: Flags as the observable result
model.body: After a logic instruction the processor clears $CF$ and $OF$ and updates $ZF$, $SF$ and $PF$ from the result. $\texttt{TEST}$ performs the AND but discards the result, so only the flags change; $ZF$ is $1$ when the tested bit is clear. A shift moves the last bit that leaves the register into $CF$, which turns $\texttt{SHR}$ into a bit reader.

model.heading: Shift counts on the 8086
model.body: The original 8086 accepts an immediate shift count of $1$ only. Any larger count must be placed in $\texttt{CL}$, for example $\texttt{MOV CL, 6}$ followed by $\texttt{SHR AL, CL}$. Boundary case: a count of $0$ leaves the operand and the flags untouched.

model.heading: Segments, stack and memory
model.body: Memory is addressed as a segment and an offset, and the physical address is formed by shifting the segment left by four bits and adding the offset, so the space is $2^{20}$ bytes. The stack grows downward: $\texttt{PUSH}$ decrements $\texttt{SP}$ by $2$ before storing a word, and $\texttt{POP}$ increments it after loading. Code lives in the code segment, initialised data in the data segment, and the stack in its own segment, which is the 8086 analogue of the .text, .data and stack regions.

Clear a bit with AND and the complemented mask.
Toggle a bit with XOR.
TEST sets the zero flag from the masked bit without changing the register.
Read a bit with a right shift and a mask, or through the carry flag.

mapping.body: Chooses the real-mode 8086 engine. The editor then offers the low-level inspector tabs instead of the variable view.

Shows $\texttt{AX}$, $\texttt{BX}$, $\texttt{CX}$, $\texttt{DX}$ and the pointer and segment registers; the HEX, DEC and BIN selector changes the radix so the individual bits $b_n$ of the result can be read directly.
$ZF$, $CF$, $SF$, $OF$ and $PF$ light up according to the last instruction, giving the result of $\texttt{TEST}$ and of the bit shifted out by $\texttt{SHR}$.
Single-stepping executes one instruction, so the transformation $AL \to AL'$ of each equation can be checked line by line; breakpoints stop at a chosen instruction.
Lists the words pushed at $\texttt{SS:SP}$ and shows the stack pointer moving by $2$ per word.
Displays bytes at a chosen reference address in hex, decimal or binary, so a memory-mapped style byte can be modified with the same mask idioms.
Records each executed instruction with the register changes, which documents the sequence of mask operations.

example.title: Edit the byte $\texttt{AL}$ with four mask instructions
example.problem: Start from $AL = \texttt{0A5h}$. Set bit $3$, clear bit $2$, toggle bit $7$, then test bit $5$ and read it through the carry flag.

steps.text: Set bit $3$: the mask is $2^{3} = \texttt{08h}$, and $\texttt{OR AL, 08h}$ gives
Clear bit $2$: the complement of $2^{2} = \texttt{04h}$ is $\texttt{0FBh}$, and $\texttt{AND AL, 0FBh}$ gives
Toggle bit $7$: the mask is $2^{7} = \texttt{80h}$, and $\texttt{XOR AL, 80h}$ gives
Test bit $5$ with $\texttt{TEST AL, 20h}$: the AND result is $\texttt{29h} \mathbin{\&} \texttt{20h} = \texttt{20h}$, which is non-zero, so $ZF = 0$ and the bit is set.
Read the same bit through the carry: after $\texttt{MOV CL, 6}$ and $\texttt{SHR AL, CL}$ the last bit shifted out is $b_5$, so $CF = 1$ and $AL = \texttt{00h}$.

example.result: The byte evolves $\texttt{A5h} \to \texttt{ADh} \to \texttt{A9h} \to \texttt{29h}$, the test reports $ZF = 0$, and the shift leaves $CF = 1$ and $AL = \texttt{00h}$.

applications.body: Many installed PC-based machine controllers and boot firmware still use real-mode assembly, where output ports are driven by setting and clearing single bits of a byte.
Early boot code configures hardware through masked read-modify-write sequences on port registers, exactly the $\texttt{OR}$ and $\texttt{AND}$ patterns shown here.
The register, flag and stack model transfers directly to embedded cores, which makes the 8086 a clear first model of a processor.
Reading status bytes with $\texttt{TEST}$ and decoding flag words is the daily work of firmware debugging and fault analysis.

python.title: Python Mode: Integer Bit Operations and the Memory Model
python.intro: This mode runs Python and traces each statement, so bit operations on integers and the objects behind variables can be watched step by step.
python.purpose: The editor executes a Python script and reports variables, the execution trace and telemetry. Because Python integers are objects of unlimited width, the bit idioms used for registers in C carry over unchanged in form, $\texttt{x |= (1 << n)}$, $\texttt{x \&= \textasciitilde(1 << n)}$, $\texttt{x \textasciicircum= (1 << n)}$ and $\texttt{(x >> n) \& 1}$, but the meaning of the complement and of overflow is different, and fixed-width hardware registers must be emulated explicitly.

model.heading: Bitwise operators on arbitrary-precision integers
model.body: An integer $x$ is treated as an infinite two's complement bit string, so the operators $\texttt{|}$, $\texttt{\&}$, $\texttt{<<}$ and $\texttt{>>}$ never overflow. A left shift by $n$ multiplies by $2^{n}$ and a right shift floors the division by $2^{n}$, including for negative numbers.

model.heading: The complement is negative
model.body: The operator $\sim$ obeys $\sim x = -x - 1$, so $\sim 0$ is $-1$ and not a mask of ones with a fixed width. Clearing a bit with $x \mathbin{\&} \sim(1 \ll n)$ still works because the infinite sign extension supplies ones above the mask, but printing the complement alone yields a negative number.

model.heading: Emulating a fixed-width register
model.body: To model a register of $w$ bits, apply the mask $2^{w} - 1$ after every operation. Boundary case: for $w = 8$ the mask is $255$, so $\sim 54$ becomes $201$ after masking.

model.heading: Memory model and ctypes
model.body: Names are references to heap objects and the call stack holds frames, so there is no direct control of sections or addresses. For memory-mapped style experiments the standard module $\texttt{ctypes}$ offers fixed-width types such as $\texttt{c\_uint8}$ and structures with bit fields, which pack the bits $b_i$ into the layout given by the sum of $b_i \, 2^{i}$.

Clear bit n with AND and the complemented mask.
Toggle bit n with XOR.
Read bit n by shifting and masking.
Python complement identity and masking to a fixed width w.
Positional expansion of an integer and the population count.

applications.body: Engineers prototype register-handling logic in Python before porting it to C, using integer masks to model status and control registers.
Fieldbus and sensor frames pack flags into bytes, and Python scripts decode them with shifts and masks in commissioning tools.
Encoders and inertial sensors deliver packed words that are unpacked with the same bitwise expressions.
Test scripts drive digital outputs and read status bits of a device under test through masked operations.

cpp.title: C++ Mode: Typed Bit Manipulation and Zero-Cost Registers
cpp.intro: This mode compiles and steps through C++ programs, where the same bit idioms are wrapped in types, constants and templates without extra run-time cost.
cpp.purpose: The editor executes a C++ program and shows its variables, trace and telemetry. The register idioms are identical to C: set $\texttt{REG |= (1UL << n)}$, clear $\texttt{REG \&= \textasciitilde(1UL << n)}$, toggle $\texttt{REG \textasciicircum= (1UL << n)}$ and read $\texttt{(REG >> n) \& 1UL}$. C++ adds tools that make them safer, namely $\texttt{constexpr}$ masks, scoped enumerations, $\texttt{std::bitset}$ and template wrappers around a $\texttt{volatile}$ pointer.

model.heading: Masks evaluated at compile time
model.body: A $\texttt{constexpr}$ function can compute the mask $M$ of a set of bit positions $S$ as the sum of the powers $2^{i}$, so the generated code contains a single constant. Using a mask for several bits at once lets one OR, AND or XOR change the whole set, and the number of affected bits equals the cardinality $\vert S \vert$.

model.heading: Typed access to hardware
model.body: A register can be modelled as a class holding a $\texttt{volatile}$ pointer obtained from an integer address, as in $\texttt{reinterpret\_cast<volatile uint32\_t*>(0x40020014)}$. Every member function performs one read-modify-write. Because the qualifier is kept, the optimiser still may not cache or drop accesses.

model.heading: Bit containers and shift limits
model.body: The container $\texttt{std::bitset}$ provides $\texttt{set}$, $\texttt{reset}$, $\texttt{flip}$ and $\texttt{test}$, which map one to one onto the four idioms. As in C, a shift by $n \ge w$ on a type of $w$ bits is undefined, so the index must stay in $0 \le n \le w - 1$.

model.heading: Sections, stack and heap
model.body: Objects with static storage are placed in $\texttt{.data}$ or $\texttt{.bss}$, and $\texttt{constexpr}$ tables go to $\texttt{.rodata}$. Automatic objects use the stack, while $\texttt{new}$ uses the heap. Constructors of global objects run before $\texttt{main}$, which costs start-up time and RAM that the budget equation must include.

applications.body: Template register wrappers give compile-time checked access to peripherals with the same machine code as hand-written C.
Real-time frameworks use typed flag sets to represent drive states and fault words without run-time overhead.
Restricted C++ subsets use constants and strong types to prevent mixing of register widths and offsets.
Bit containers decode packed digital input words from field devices into named signals.

c.title: C Mode: Register Bit Manipulation and Memory Sections
c.intro: This mode compiles and steps through C programs, which makes it the natural place to practise the bit idioms and the memory layout of embedded firmware.
c.purpose: The editor executes a C program and presents its variables, execution trace, telemetry and a quick reference. The four fundamental register idioms are set $\texttt{REG |= (1UL << n)}$, clear $\texttt{REG \&= \textasciitilde(1UL << n)}$, toggle $\texttt{REG \textasciicircum= (1UL << n)}$ and read $\texttt{(REG >> n) \& 1UL}$. Around them sit the concepts that decide whether such code is correct on a real microcontroller: the qualifier $\texttt{volatile}$, memory-mapped pointers, the program sections and the split between stack and heap.

model.heading: Read-modify-write with a mask
model.body: Each idiom builds a mask $1 \ll n$ with an unsigned constant so that the shift is not performed on a signed type. Boundary case: shifting by $n \ge w$ for a type of $w$ bits is undefined, so $n$ must satisfy $0 \le n \le w - 1$. Multi-bit fields are inserted with the width mask $M_w = 2^{w} - 1$ after clearing the old field.

model.heading: volatile and memory-mapped I/O
model.body: A peripheral register is reached through a fixed address, for example $\texttt{*(volatile uint32\_t*)0x40020014}$. The qualifier $\texttt{volatile}$ forbids the compiler from caching the value in a CPU register or removing accesses, because the hardware may change the content at any time and each write has a side effect. In this simulator such addresses are illustrative, since the program runs on an emulated engine and not on a physical peripheral.

model.heading: Program sections
model.body: The linker places instructions in $\texttt{.text}$ and constants in $\texttt{.rodata}$, both in flash. Initialised globals live in $\texttt{.data}$, whose initial image is stored in flash and copied to RAM at start-up, while zero-initialised globals live in $\texttt{.bss}$ and are cleared. The sums above show that $\texttt{.data}$ is counted in both memories.

model.heading: Stack versus heap
model.body: Local variables and return addresses use the stack, which grows toward the heap in the same RAM. Dynamic allocation uses the heap and can fragment, so embedded designs bound $S_{stack}$ and often avoid the heap. A collision of the two regions corrupts data silently.

applications.body: GPIO, timer and UART peripherals are configured by masked updates of memory-mapped registers declared $\texttt{volatile}$.
Engine and drive controllers pack status flags into words that are set, cleared and polled by the idioms shown here.
Coding standards demand bounded stack use, no heap, and explicit unsigned masks, which follow directly from the memory model.
Protocol headers and control words are built from bit fields inserted with width masks.
